subject: orthopaedics
title: Radial Nerve Injury and Wrist Drop

steps.tx: **Radial nerve** arises as the largest terminal branch of the posterior cord of the brachial plexus, carrying motor and sensory fibres derived from C5, C6, C7, C8, and T1 nerve roots. In the arm, it enters the spiral groove (radial groove) on the posterior aspect of the humerus, running obliquely between the medial and lateral heads of the triceps brachii. Here, the nerve lies in direct contact with the humeral periosteum before piercing the lateral intermuscular septum.
steps.say: The radial nerve originates from the posterior cord. It travels in the spiral groove behind the humerus, resting directly against the bone between the triceps heads before piercing into the anterior compartment.

steps.tx: **Holstein-Lewis fracture** refers to a spiral fracture of the distal third of the humeral shaft that carries an exceptionally high incidence of radial nerve entrapment or laceration, reaching twenty-two percent. As the distal bone fragment displaces proximally and radially, the radial nerve is trapped, stretched, or impaled against the fracture ends where it is tethered piercing the lateral intermuscular septum. Closed reduction attempts in these fractures risk crushing the entrapped nerve.
steps.say: The Holstein-Lewis fracture is a spiral fracture of the distal third of the humerus. The radial nerve is tethered as it pierces the lateral intermuscular septum, placing it at high risk of entrapment between bone fragments.

vis.title: Mechanisms and Levels of Radial Nerve Lesions
rows: Finger drop; wrist extension spared with radial deviation

steps.tx: **Wrist drop** represents the cardinal motor physical manifestation of radial nerve injury at or distal to the spiral groove. Denervation of the primary wrist extensors (extensor carpi radialis longus, extensor carpi radialis brevis, and extensor carpi ulnaris) deprives the wrist of active extension. Simultaneously, paralysis of extensor digitorum communis, extensor indicis proprius, and extensor digiti minimi causes complete inability to extend the fingers at the metacarpophalangeal joints, alongside paralysis of thumb extension and abduction.
steps.say: Wrist drop is the hallmark of radial nerve palsy. The patient cannot extend the wrist, fingers, or thumb because all extensor muscles are paralyzed. In spiral groove injuries, triceps extension is preserved.

steps.tx: **Intrinsic hand muscles** maintain active extension of the proximal and distal interphalangeal joints despite complete radial nerve paralysis. The lumbricals and interossei are innervated by the median and ulnar nerves, inserting into the extensor expansions of the digits. When the examiner manually supports the patient metacarpophalangeal joints in neutral extension, the patient can fully extend the interphalangeal joints, demonstrating that interphalangeal extension is preserved by uninjured intrinsic hand muscles.
steps.say: Crucially, patients with radial nerve palsy can still extend their interphalangeal finger joints if the knuckles are supported. This movement is powered by the lumbricals and interossei, which are median and ulnar-innervated.

steps.tx: **Dorsal first web space** represents the sole autonomous sensory territory of the superficial radial nerve. Sensory testing over the small cutaneous patch on the dorsum of the hand between the first and second metacarpals provides rapid bedside confirmation of radial nerve integrity. Extensive peripheral cutaneous overlap from the lateral antebrachial cutaneous, median, and ulnar nerves minimizes sensory deficits across the remainder of the dorsal forearm and hand.
steps.say: Test sensation on the dorsal web space between the thumb and index finger. This is the only autonomous sensory patch of the radial nerve. The rest of the dorsal hand has overlapping nerves that mask sensory loss.

steps.tx: **Closed humerus fracture** with immediate radial nerve palsy is managed expectantly because the underlying neural pathology represents neurapraxia or axonotmesis in over eighty-five percent of cases. Spontaneous neurological recovery occurs in nearly ninety percent of patients within three to four months. Initial management consists of closed fracture reduction, functional bracing or splinting, and application of a dynamic cock-up wrist splint to prevent wrist flexion contracture while awaiting axonal re-innervation.
steps.say: Over eighty-five percent of radial nerve palsies in closed humerus fractures are bruises or stretch injuries that heal on their own. Support the wrist in a dynamic cock-up splint and watch for recovery over three to four months.

steps.tx: **Dynamic cock-up splint** supports the paralyzed wrist in thirty degrees of extension while incorporating spring-loaded elastic outriggers that extend the metacarpophalangeal joints. This orthosis maintains the wrist in its optimal functional position, which dramatically enhances finger flexor grasp strength. Without a splint, wrist drop produces profound passive insufficiency of the finger flexors, rendering the hand virtually useless for grasping objects despite intact median and ulnar motor function.
steps.say: A dynamic cock-up splint holds the wrist in extension so the intact median and ulnar flexors can grip objects. Without wrist extension, passive flexor insufficiency leaves the patient unable to make a strong fist.

steps.tx: **Triple tendon transfer** is the definitive surgical reconstruction for permanent, irreversible radial nerve palsy failing to show electrodiagnostic or clinical recovery after twelve months. The standard classic tendon transfer triad transfers the pronator teres to extensor carpi radialis brevis to restore wrist extension; flexor carpi radialis or flexor carpi ulnaris to extensor digitorum communis to restore finger extension; and palmaris longus to extensor pollicis longus to restore thumb extension.
steps.say: For permanent radial nerve palsy, perform a triple tendon transfer: pronator teres restores wrist extension, flexor carpi radialis restores finger extension, and palmaris longus restores thumb extension, giving full hand function.
